name: Prize crossword No 24,957
preamble: Five across and ten down solutions are themed and may not be further defined

indicators.note: a span stretches across something, so the run of letters bridges the gap between two words

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word plus the start of the second

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark invites a quip about short concentration, but the letters sit across the join of 'Low' and 'attention'. The answer is a unit of power, one of the puzzle's themed measures, so it gets no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries are left undefined; this one is the SI unit of power, named after James Watt the engineer.

clue.text: Old Queen of Castile forgetting to study lines

indicators.note: to forget something is to leave it out, so a piece is dropped from the name

blocks.note: Constanza (Constance) of Castile, a medieval queen and wife of John of Gaunt
to con is an old word meaning to study or learn by heart

explanation.surface: A historical queen of Castile neglects her studies of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping CON from the front of CONSTANZA leaves STANZA. 'Con' for study is old-fashioned but a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: A stanza is a group of verse lines forming a unit within a poem, like a paragraph in prose.

clue.text: Hence improvement, having swallowed tablets in dish

indicators.note: whatever has been swallowed ends up inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: so means therefore, hence
an upturn is an improvement in fortunes
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet; two of them make the plural

explanation.surface: Things got better after some pills were taken with a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: UPTURN swallows EE between its last two letters, then SO goes in front. E for an ecstasy pill is a common crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A soup tureen is a large deep serving bowl with a lid, a type of dish used at table.

indicators.note: one thing being inside another means it goes within the other's letters

blocks.note: nineteen in Roman numerals
Mae West, the Hollywood actress

explanation.walkthrough: '19' looks like a cross-reference to another clue but is just a number in Roman numerals. A measure can be a dance, and this Brazilian dance is one of the themed entries, so it is undefined.
explanation.definitionFit: The maxixe is a Brazilian ballroom dance resembling the tango, and an old meaning of measure is a stately dance.

clue.text: More mature, we dipped into "Lady Chatterley's Lover", not quite climaxing?

indicators.note: falling just short of the end means the final letter is lost
something dipped into a thing goes inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
Oliver Mellors is the gamekeeper who is Lady Chatterley's lover in D H Lawrence's novel

explanation.surface: A saucy confession of reading a racy novel without quite reaching the end.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks suggest the book title, but the lover is the character, the gamekeeper in D H Lawrence's banned novel. 'Climaxing' is a racy way of saying reaching the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellow describes something softened and ripened by age, so the comparative form means more mature.

indicators.note: going into something puts it within, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
an ace is the one in a pack of cards

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like streams merging, but it is R placed inside ACE. The answer, a unit of land area, is one of the undefined themed measures.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries are not defined; this is the traditional unit of land area, 4,840 square yards.

clue.text: Sensational spin bowled by everyone to lout, non-amateur

indicators.note: without an amateur means the letter standing for amateur is taken out

blocks.note: B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
all means everyone
a yahoo is a boorish lout, from Swift's Gulliver's Travels
A is the abbreviation for amateur

explanation.surface: A cricket report: a sensational spin delivery bowled to a lout who is no amateur.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin' and 'bowled' set up a cricket scene, but spin here is publicity. YAHOO loses its A to give YHOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballyhoo is extravagant publicity or hype, the kind of sensational promotional spin used to drum up interest.

blocks.note: taken as written
CH is the international code for Switzerland (Confoederatio Helvetica)

explanation.surface: Somewhere in landlocked Switzerland there is a little island.
explanation.walkthrough: Also a themed unit of length, but here it is defined by its Scottish sense; Switzerland is CH on car stickers.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland and Ireland an inch is a small island, from Gaelic innis, as in many place names.

clue.text: It's a short walk to Lincoln to see old instrument

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is lopped off

blocks.note: taken as written
a stroll is a leisurely walk
Abe Lincoln, US president

explanation.surface: A short stroll takes you to see an antique in the city of Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln looks like the English cathedral city, but it is Abraham Lincoln shortened to ABE.
explanation.definitionFit: The astrolabe was a medieval astronomical device for measuring the altitude of stars, used in early navigation.

clue.text: Charlie has no place in M&S, say

indicators.note: having none of something means it is removed

blocks.note: Charlie Chaplin, the silent film comedian
PL is the abbreviation for place in street names

explanation.surface: Someone called Charlie can't find a place in Marks & Spencer.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie wants to be C in the radio alphabet; it is Chaplin. M&S is Marks & Spencer, a British high-street retailer with stores nationwide.
explanation.definitionFit: Marks & Spencer is an example of a retail chain, a group of shops under common ownership.

clue.text: Fashion's getting pricier and may possibly go fast

blocks.note: ton means fashion or style, from French; the 's is 'has'
prices that are up have risen

explanation.surface: Fashion keeps getting more expensive and may soon be a passing fad.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton-up is British slang for a motorcyclist who rides at 100 mph, a 'ton'; the definition hedges with 'may possibly' because not every such rider is speeding.
explanation.definitionFit: Ton-up describes a speed-loving motorcycle rider, someone liable to travel at a hundred miles an hour.

blocks.note: surface reading: an impoverished nation or condition
setter's reading: the two words of the phrase nearly cancel each other out

explanation.surface: A struggling country that is nearly a paradox.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase pairs a word for sickness with the word for wellbeing, so it comes close to being an oxymoron.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unwell is a poor physical condition, a state of the body that is not good.

blocks.note: surface reading: the long-running BBC television drama strand
setter's reading: a Shakespeare play suiting today's puzzle, whose theme is units

explanation.walkthrough: Play for Today was a BBC series of one-off TV dramas; here it means a play that fits this puzzle's theme, the Shakespeare comedy whose title repeats the theme word.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespeare comedy about justice in Vienna is a play, and its title names the theme of this crossword.

clue.text: Roman soldier in Malta lies injured

indicators.note: something injured is damaged out of its proper shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: M is the international vehicle code for Malta
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wounded legionary lies hurt on Malta.
explanation.walkthrough: Miles is the Latin word for a soldier; it is also a themed unit, used by 19 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Miles is the Latin noun for soldier, the term for a Roman legionary or foot soldier.

clue.text: They're beginning to win on Thames ground

definitions.note: a team is referred to in the plural

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter
ground down means crushed and reworked into a new form

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A London football team starting to win at their riverside home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a football stadium but signals the anagram. West Ham United is a London football club near the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: West Ham is a football club, a group of players who can be called they, just as fans speak of a team.

indicators.note: a sort of something is a version of it, so these letters form a variant

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something produces milk, more or less.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: a cave formation hangs and drips milky mineral water, rather like an udder.
explanation.definitionFit: A stalactite grows by dripping calcium-rich water from a cave roof, so it oozes a milky liquid of a kind.

clue.text: Monsieur has to be in his own country

indicators.note: the phrase marks the next word to be given in a foreign language

blocks.note: M. is the abbreviation for Monsieur
être is French for to be

explanation.surface: A Frenchman longs to be back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In his own country' tells us to translate into French. The answer is a themed unit of length, so there is no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries go undefined; this is the SI base unit of length, defined via the speed of light.

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: to tell stories is to lie
TR is the international code for Turkey

explanation.surface: Someone spins yarns about Turkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turkey' looks like the bird or the meal, but it is the country code TR. The answer, a metric unit of volume, is a themed entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries go undefined; this is the metric unit of capacity, a thousand cubic centimetres.

clue.text: I met Neil producing "The History Cycle" perhaps

indicators.note: to produce a work is to create something new out of material, so the letters are reformed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Meeting a TV producer who made a history series.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Producing' looks like a TV producer's credit, but it reworks the letters. The History Cycle sounds like a documentary series, an example of history laid out in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A timeline lays out events in chronological sequence, so a chronicle of history could be described as one.

blocks.note: surface reading: a sum built from other clue numbers
setter's reading: the 13 entry is a distance unit, so this is how many of a shorter unit make two of them

explanation.walkthrough: 13 down is MILES, so '2 13' is two miles; a mile is eight of the wanted unit, so sixteen fit in two.
explanation.definitionFit: There are eight of these horse-racing distance units in a mile, each 220 yards long, so sixteen in two.

blocks.note: taken as written
the standard rule, or ruler, is twelve inches long, the imperial unit for that length

explanation.surface: Things that usually occur, as a general principle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' reads as 'usually', but a rule is a ruler, and the common one measures a foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Something afoot is going on or in progress, so the word describes events under way at present.

indicators.note: a baffled mind is confused and scrambled, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A class of students stays puzzled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remains' reads as a verb, stays, but it supplies the letters, and 'baffled' reorders them.
explanation.definitionFit: A seminar is a small university class where students meet with a tutor to discuss a topic.

clue.text: A thousand in cash or half that

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: K is short for a thousand, as in a salary of 50K
cash is money

explanation.surface: Someone's asking a grand in cash, or settling for half.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That' refers back to a thousand pounds; British slang calls £500 a monkey.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a monkey is five hundred pounds, which is exactly half of a thousand.

clue.text: Odd venue arranged to host Beethoven's Ninth

indicators.note: the ninth is the letter in position nine of the word
to arrange is to put in a new order
a host takes in guests, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: taken as written
the ninth letter of the name

explanation.surface: A strange concert hall is set up to stage Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: Beethoven's Ninth looks like the choral symphony, but it is the ninth letter of his name, which the rearranged venue holds at its end.
explanation.definitionFit: Odd and uneven are synonyms for numbers not divisible by two, or things irregular and unbalanced.

blocks.note: surface reading: two clue numbers, or simply two numbers added
setter's reading: two shillings and sixpence in pre-decimal British money

explanation.walkthrough: The numbers look like cross-references to 2 and 6 down; they are old money, two shillings and six pence, a coin withdrawn after decimalisation in 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: The old British coin worth two shillings and sixpence was an eighth of a pound, in use until decimal currency arrived.

clue.text: When river drops river horses find fruit

indicators.note: dropping something means letting it go, so letters are removed

blocks.note: hippopotamus is Greek for river horse
the Po is the main river of northern Italy

explanation.surface: When the river level falls, hippos go looking for something to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The second river is the definition of the first word's meaning: HIPPOS loses PO.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose hips are the red fruits left on rose bushes after flowering, used for syrup and tea.

indicators.note: ropy, or ropey, is British slang for shoddy or in poor shape, so the letters are out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tatty sack used to hold things.
explanation.walkthrough: Ropy looks like it describes a sack made of rope; it is British slang for poor quality.
explanation.definitionFit: A cask is a barrel, a wooden vessel used to hold liquids such as beer or wine.

clue.text: Somerville and Ross collection ignored Irish

indicators.note: what is ignored is left out, so a word goes

blocks.note: Some Experiences of an Irish R.M. was a story collection by Somerville and Ross, often called The Irish R.M.
taken as written

explanation.surface: A literary collection by two authors leaves out its Irish setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Somerville and Ross were two Irish women writers; their comic stories of a resident magistrate are known as The Irish R.M. The answer, a unit of heat, is a themed entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries go undefined; this is a unit of heat once used for gas bills, a hundred thousand British thermal units.

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
olé is the shout of a bullfight crowd, written here without its accent

explanation.surface: The bullfighter gets the crowd's first cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Accentless' simply licenses dropping the accent from olé. The answer is the SI unit of amount of substance, a themed entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries go undefined; this is the SI unit of chemical quantity, about six times ten to the twenty-third particles.

indicators.note: something missing is absent, so it is taken out

blocks.note: points means indicates
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Signals that nothing has gone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: POINTS loses its O. The answer, a unit of liquid volume, is a themed entry, so the clue has no definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Theme entries go undefined; these are imperial units of liquid capacity, familiar from beer and milk in Britain.

clue.text: Fabulous bargain is what every card player wants

blocks.note: first meaning: a terrific bargain
second meaning: a fine hand dealt out in a card game

explanation.surface: A superb bargain is what every gambler at the table hopes for.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads first as shopping, then as the cards a dealer hands round.
explanation.definitionFit: A bargain is a deal, and in cards the deal is the distribution of hands, which every player wants to be good.
